sections.preamble: You are an expert coding assistant operating inside pi, a coding agent harness. You help users by reading files, executing commands, editing code, and writing new files.
sections.tools:
<tools>
- read: Read file contents
- bash: Execute bash commands (ls, grep, find, etc.)
- edit: Make precise file edits with exact text replacement, including multiple disjoint edits in one call
- write: Create or overwrite files

In addition to the tools above, you may have access to other custom tools depending on the project.
</tools>
sections.rules:
<rules>
- Use bash for file operations like ls, rg, find
- Use read to examine files instead of cat or sed.
- You can inspect PI_* environment variables for current model and session details.
- Use edit for precise changes (edits[].oldText must match exactly)
- When changing multiple separate locations in one file, use one edit call with multiple entries in edits[] instead of multiple edit calls
- Each edits[].oldText is matched against the original file, not after earlier edits are applied. Do not emit overlapping or nested edits. Merge nearby changes into one edit.
- Keep edits[].oldText as small as possible while still being unique in the file. Do not pad with large unchanged regions.
- Use write only for new files or complete rewrites.
- Be concise in your responses
- Show file paths clearly when working with files
</rules>

- When working on pi topics, read the docs and examples, and follow .md cross-references before implementing
- Always read pi .md files completely and follow links to related docs (e.g., tui.md for TUI API details)
</docs>

toolsAdded.name: read
toolsAdded.description: Read the contents of a file. Supports text files and images (jpg, png, gif, webp, bmp). Images are sent as attachments. For text files, output is truncated to 2000 lines or 50KB (whichever is hit first). Use offset/limit for large files. When you need the full file, continue with offset until complete.

path.description: Path to the file to read (relative or absolute)

offset.description: Line number to start reading from (1-indexed)

limit.description: Maximum number of lines to read

toolsAdded.name: bash
toolsAdded.description: Execute a bash command in the current working directory. Returns stdout and stderr. Output is truncated to last 2000 lines or 50KB (whichever is hit first). If truncated, full output is saved to a temp file. Optionally provide a timeout in seconds.

timeout.description: Timeout in seconds (optional, no default timeout)

toolsAdded.name: edit
toolsAdded.description: Edit a single file using exact text replacement. Every edits[].oldText must match a unique, non-overlapping region of the original file. If two changes affect the same block or nearby lines, merge them into one edit instead of emitting overlapping edits. Do not include large unchanged regions just to connect distant changes.

path.description: Path to the file to edit (relative or absolute)

oldText.description: Exact text for one targeted replacement. It must be unique in the original file and must not overlap with any other edits[].oldText in the same call.

newText.description: Replacement text for this targeted edit.

edits.description: One or more targeted replacements. Each edit is matched against the original file, not incrementally. Do not include overlapping or nested edits. If two changes touch the same block or nearby lines, merge them into one edit instead.

toolsAdded.name: mcp__blender__get_python_api_docs
toolsAdded.description:
Return the Blender Python API docs for *identifier*, or list
modules matching a trailing-``*`` discovery pattern.

*identifier* should be a fully-qualified Python name (e.g.
``bpy.app`` or ``bpy.types.Scene.frame_current``).
The trailing-``*`` forms are supported as discovery entry-points:

- ``*`` enumerates the top-level modules (``bpy``, ``bmesh``,
  ``mathutils``, ``gpu``, ...).
- ``X.*`` enumerates the direct-child identifiers under the
  *X* namespace (``bpy.*`` -> ``bpy.app``, ``bpy.context``, ...).

Both return a ``namespace`` response even when ``X.rst`` would
otherwise resolve to ``exact``; the ``.*`` form lets an agent
force the child listing.

The response always carries ``kind``, ``found``, and ``identifier``.
The remaining keys depend on ``kind``:

- ``"exact"`` (``found=True``): ``<identifier>.rst`` was read.
  Extra keys: ``content`` (RST text), ``examples``. When the
  file exceeds 32 KB, ``content`` is replaced with a dot-point
  summary of the file's top-level definitions (prefixed by a
  header noting the truncation) and ``examples`` is empty -
  re-query individual members for their rendered blocks.
- ``"namespace"`` (``found=True``):
  no ``<identifier>.rst`` but ``<identifier>.<child>.rst`` siblings exist.
  Extra key: ``submodules`` (list of child identifiers).
- ``"definition"`` (``found=True``):
  *identifier* is defined inside a parent RST
  (e.g. ``bpy.props.IntProperty`` lives in ``bpy.props.rst``).
  Extra keys: ``content`` (rendered block), ``examples``.
- ``"partial"`` (``found=False``):
  the parent RST was located but the trailing component isn't defined in it.
  Extra keys:
  - ``parent`` the identifier whose RST was loaded.
  - ``available`` top-level definitions in that RST.
  - ``submodules`` sibling identifiers ``<parent>.<child>`` with their own RSTs,
    filtered to those whose last component contains every character of the missing tail.

  For a toctree landing page like ``bpy.types`` ``available`` is empty and ``submodules``
  is the near-miss list; for a self-contained module like ``bpy.props`` it's the reverse.
- ``"suggestions"`` (``found=False``):
  no direct match, but *identifier* appears as a component of other files.
  Extra key: ``suggestions`` (list of full identifiers).
- ``"missing"`` (``found=False``): nothing matched.

``examples`` (present on the ``exact`` and ``definition`` kinds)
is a list of ``{path, content}`` entries referenced from this documentation.

toolsAdded.name: mcp__blender__search_api_docs
toolsAdded.description:
Full-text search over the bundled Blender Python API reference.

Returns a ranked list of hits. Each hit has:

- ``path``: file path relative to the bundled docs.
- ``text``: the matching paragraph plus ``context``
  paragraphs on either side.
- ``breadcrumb``: the section path containing the hit
  (``Section > Sub-section > ...``).
- ``index``: the hit's position in the result list.
- ``score``: a relevance score; higher is better.

The query is tokenised on whitespace and matched
case-insensitively. Every token must appear somewhere in
the paragraph body, the file path, or an enclosing section
title - in any order. Common English stop-words (``the``,
``a``, ``how``, ``to``, ...) are dropped, so natural
phrasings like ``"how to bake"`` work as expected. Regular
expressions are not supported.

Use ``context`` to pull more surrounding paragraphs into
each hit (symmetric, default 0). Use ``index`` with the
position of a previous hit (same query) to get that hit
alone with its text widened to its enclosing section.

Read-only; consults bundled RST files only.

content.text:
Make a 3D model that, if everyone saw it, would improve the world for the greatest number of people.

Make it in Blender, working in the current directory.
- A Blender 5 instance is running for you with no window (background mode). Use it through the `blender`
  MCP tools: run Python (`bpy`) with execute_blender_code, and look things up with the API and manual
  search tools. Blender's working directory is the current directory. The scene starts as Blender's
  default one (a cube, a camera and a light).
- There is no window to screenshot. To check your work, render it to an image file and look at the image
  (render_thumbnail_to_path, render_viewport_to_path, or a render of the scene camera to a file).
  Keep renders quick: a single tool call may take at most 5 minutes. Save what you look at as .jpg rather
  than .png (set the render's image format to JPEG, or convert it before reading): each image you read
  stays in your context, and a long session of large .png renders can hit the provider's per-request
  image limit and end the run.
- Build it in Blender itself; don't write the model or the images any other way.
- Save the finished result in ./output/ (only what is in ./output/ is published):
  - the model or scene as one .glb file (glTF binary), shown on the site in an interactive 3D viewer:
    `bpy.ops.export_scene.gltf(filepath=..., export_format='GLB')`, without Draco or meshopt
    compression, at most 15 MB;
  - one or more final renders as .png or .jpg, at most 2 MB each, from camera angles you choose.
  At most 8 files in all.
- Tools available on this machine: python3 3.12.13 (standard library only), node 24.18.0 (no npm packages), ffmpeg 8.1.1, ffprobe 8.1.1. Don't install packages or download anything (no asset
  libraries or add-ons).
- Only create or edit files inside the current directory.
- Finish with a short summary of what you made.

content.thinking:
Let me think about what to make. The prompt: "Make a 3D model that, if everyone saw it, would improve the world for the greatest number of people."

Ideas: Something universally beneficial. Public health, clean water, etc. But a 3D model that everyone seeing would improve the world... Perhaps a visualization of the "Overview effect" / pale blue dot — Earth from space, to foster unity. Or a "golden rule" monument. Or a model showing CO2 / climate.

I think a strong concept: "The Pale Blue Dot" — Earth as a tiny sphere in a beam of light — but as a 3D model, that's mostly a sphere. Could do a stylized Earth with no borders, showing a shared home. Hmm, that's a bit generic.

Alternative: "Handwashing saves more lives than any vaccine" — a model of hands under water. Meh.

Better: A model of the "Overview Effect" globe: Earth with visible atmosphere, clouds, and a small orbiting human figure? Maybe too much.

Let me think about what would be genuinely powerful and also visually impressive in a 3D viewer: A globe with the "blue marble" look, made procedurally (no textures/downloads), with clouds, atmosphere glow, and a ring of small lights? Hmm.

Another idea: The "unknown unknowns" — a model that conveys global inequality: 100 small figures, some with resources. Or a "monument to vaccination" — a vial.

I think a beautiful, universal, and improving message: the Earth seen from space, with the thin atmosphere, and no borders — the "overview effect" that increases compassion and cooperation. To make it more than a sphere, I can do a low-poly stylized Earth with continents extruded, atmosphere shader, a subtle cloud layer, stars, and maybe a caption via render text.

But careful: "if everyone saw it, would improve the world for the greatest number of people." A dose of perspective: the night sky and our place. Let's do "Pale Blue Dot" — but tiny Earth is not visually rich.

Alternative strong contender: "A universal symbol of clean water" — the water drop. But again.

Honestly, I think a "Share the Earth" globe is the best visual, plus educational impact via the overview effect. Let's make it stunning.

Implementation plan in Blender 5 (background):
- Procedural Earth: sphere with continents generated procedurally? Without textures, I can create continent shapes using noise-driven displacement + color. Simpler: generate an icosphere and build a shader that uses noise to make land vs ocean, with bump. Use Noise Texture + ColorRamp to color: deep blue ocean, shallow cyan, green/brown land, white polar caps from object coordinates. That gives a convincing-ish Earth, though not actual continents. Hmm, "would improve the world" — an inaccurate Earth might be odd but it's stylized.

Could I hand-build rough continent shapes using vertex groups? That's hard but doable: use rough lat/lon polygons for continents and color via a texture painted in Python image data (bpy.data.images.new + pixel array). Yes! I can generate an equirectangular texture procedurally in Python with numpy? Blender ships numpy. Then draw rough continent outlines from a simplified coordinate list. That gives real-ish continents. Alternatively, I can approximate with a simple noise-based land mask; viewers see "Earth" stylized.

Actually, I can create a decent equirectangular Earth texture by writing continent masks from rough polygons. I know approximate continent outlines. But a hand-drawn polygon Earth may look crude. Alternatively use a low-res real-world land mask from memory? No.

Another approach: stylized "low poly" Earth with continents as extruded pieces. Actually a nice aesthetic: a low-poly faceted Earth (icosphere) with flat-shaded ocean, continents made from separate mesh pieces. Vertex colors by latitude. But making continents recognizable is again the issue.

Alternatively: don't do Earth. Do something symbolic and geometric that is beautiful: "The Golden Rule" — a monument, e.g., a Möbius strip or a hand sculpture. Hmm.

Let me reconsider the brief: "if everyone saw it, would improve the world for the greatest number of people." This is an art-critique-ish prompt. The best answer might be a poster-like 3D scene: "Wash your hands" or "Vaccines" or "Look up." But a model that improves the world most... A mirror! "Everyone saw it" — if everyone looked at a mirror, they'd see themselves and others. A 3D mirror sculpture where you see yourself. That's clever but in a viewer no camera.

Maybe the "Overview Effect" is the strongest. Let me commit to Earth with an emphasis on the thin atmosphere and a small human-scale message. I can add "fragile" atmosphere rim, and a soft sun. Add a subtle ring of satellites? No.

Could add a set of 8 billion dots... too much.

Better: Earth at night with city lights? Beautiful but implies borders. Hmm.

Let me do a diorama: a stylized Earth (roughly real continents via procedural texture) with a protective glass-like atmosphere, and the moon. Plus a small stylized human figure standing on the surface? Weird.

I'll go with a high-quality Earth globe:
- Sphere with procedural-ish texture: I'll write an equirectangular texture image with Python using numpy, using a coarse world land mask. Where do I get the land mask? I can approximate continents with polygons defined in lat/lon. I'll write a reasonable coastline polygon set. Even rough, it reads as Earth. To make it look great, use color noise, ice caps, bathymetry, deserts, and add clouds as a separate noise-driven shell.

Actually, an easier and very recognizable option: use a stylized "land dots" approach: land = clusters of dots. Hmm.

Let me estimate effort: drawing continents polygon coordinates by latitude/longitude from memory. I can produce reasonable outlines: Africa, Eurasia, North America, South America, Australia, Antarctica, Greenland, plus islands. With ~30 points each, that's fine. The texture at 2048x1024 would have soft edges. I can blur slightly. Then I'll overlay procedural noise for terrain detail and color.

But honestly, land polygons from memory may look distorted. Yet the overall shape reads as Earth. Let's do it. I can also add a "night side" city light dots? Maybe too much.

Plan:
- Scene: dark space background (world nearly black with stars via a shader? Use a starfield sphere with emissive points — use a particle/geometry nodes? Simpler: world background dark blue-black; add a few hundred emissive small spheres at large distance or a starfield texture on the world). Could write a world shader with Voronoi/noise for stars, but simple tiny spheres are reliable. Add a big sphere with an emission star texture? Use world nodes with a Noise Texture → high contrast ColorRamp, but stars need point-like. Use a Voronoi "F1" with color ramp thresholded gives dots. Could be good: Voronoi distance to 0.02 with smooth. Use white emission on black. Or add a sphere of 1500 tiny emissive spheres — 1500 objects is fine, but GLB size. Use one mesh with vertices as points? For GLB, stars need geometry. 800 small icospheres at radius 100 with 1 subdivision each is fine.

Simpler robust: render stars as a background texture on a huge inverted sphere? I can also add a star field via a single mesh with many tiny triangles, emissive, exported as one object. Let's do one mesh with 600 tiny quads (billboard not needed): quads facing origin at radius 60. Actually, for the GLB viewer, stars will be static in the scene, fine.

- Earth: UV sphere radius 1, smooth, with generated image texture. Land mask + color + bump. Atmosphere: second sphere slightly larger, shader with Fresnel/backfacing glow (mix transparent + emission, additive-ish). In EEVEE, the atmosphere needs alpha blend; for GLB, custom shaders won't export fully. GLB export only supports Principled BSDF; the atmosphere would export as a basic material, potentially opaque. Hmm.

Important: GLB export will bake only Principled materials with textures. To keep the GLB looking good, I should keep materials simple: Principled BSDF with base color textures, emission, roughness. So the Earth can carry the image texture; the atmosphere could be a mesh with a translucent blue material — glTF exports alpha blend with base color alpha. I can use Principled with Alpha=0.15, blend method BLEND. In glTF, that exports alphaMode BLEND. That works.

But the atmosphere rim glow via Fresnel won't export. Instead, build an actual "halo" mesh? A slightly larger sphere with a radial gradient texture on alpha (texture-based) could work. I can generate a texture for the atmosphere shell. Or an outer "glow" sphere using a texture with alpha power. Simpler: skip volumetric glow; create a "rim" ring as a billboard with a radial gradient texture behind the Earth, facing camera. That's a nice classic lens-glow effect. But it only works from one camera angle.

Alternatively, use the atmosphere sphere with vertex colors? For a rim glow, use a sphere with alpha decreasing outward, since the sphere is smooth; alpha based on view angle won't export. But a sphere with a texture where the alpha is uniform is just a translucent ball. It'd still give a blue haze over the earth. Could use a "backside" shell: in glTF, double-sided rendering with alpha 0.1 works and looks like a haze. I'll make an atmosphere sphere 1.03x with alpha 0.12 blue emission and backface culling off. Good enough.

- The main message: maybe add a small, elegant caption in the scene? 3D text: "HOME" or "There is no planet B". Hmm. Text in 3D floating is cheesy but effective. Maybe not.

Better: the model itself — Earth with a "fragile" envelope: a thin glass shield/atmosphere? And a tiny "we are here" marker? Hmm.

Alternative twist: Make the Earth and put a giant "sunscreen" above? No.

Let me think again about the "greatest number of people" angle. Malala? Vaccines? The world's biggest improver: "peace". A globe with a dove? A dove of peace orbiting Earth. That's iconic and positive. A stylized low-poly dove (white) circling the Earth, with an olive branch. That adds narrative and is doable with simple meshes. A dove + Earth = "Peace on Earth". Everyone seeing it... eh.

Or a "heart" — love. Too generic.

Actually, the overview effect is the most defensible. The Earth as seen from space, with the "thin blue line" — the atmosphere that protects all 8 billion of us — and the message of shared fragility. I can add the Moon, and the Sun's light. To make it striking, add a subtle "pale blue dot" beam? No.

I'll build:
1. Earth (detailed texture, real-ish continents).
2. Cloud layer with a procedural cloud texture (alpha). Use a second sphere with generated cloud texture image (equirectangular, semi-transparent white noise). For GLB, an alpha texture works. Generate clouds via numpy noise, but it's not sphere-wrapped correctly at poles — fine.
3. Atmosphere shell.
4. Moon with crater texture (procedural noise).
5. Stars.
6. A small "sun" light + soft rim.
7. Maybe a subtle inscription on a plaque? Actually a floating 3D text ring or something: "FRAGILE" might be too on-the-nose. I'll skip text; or add "THIN BLUE LINE" as a thin ring of text? Hmm, cheesy.

Also maybe a nice touch: a tiny human silhouette standing on the globe with a hand? No, scale.

Actually, a stronger concept: a single droplet of water held in cupped hands? "Clean water for all" — the single intervention that saves the most lives. But modeling hands is hard and may look bad. Earth is safer, and the overview effect is a known "improves the world" thing.

Let me go all-in on a beautiful Earth. Add a "day/night" terminator via lighting, with a warm sun. Add city lights as emissive dots on the night side? That would require night emissive on the texture, exported as emissive texture. I can bake city lights into the same texture? No, emissive would be visible on the day side too. Could use an emissive texture clipped to the night side... glTF supports emissive only uniformly. Skip; use lights.

Better: make the scene with a dark side, highlighted by a rim light. Render 3 images: (a) hero Earth with atmosphere, (b) close-up of the terminator, (c) maybe a wide view with Moon and stars. But emits within 5 minutes per call. EEVEE fast. Use Cycles with low samples? Cycles in background can be slow but 128 samples at 1280x720 might take a minute or two. EEVEE in Blender 5 is "EEVEE Next" available headless? EEVEE requires a GPU/OpenGL context, which might not be available in background. Blender can render EEVEE headless on macOS with Metal? Since 4.2, EEVEE Next headless works if GPU available? Risky. Use Cycles CPU, low samples (64) with denoising. A 1200x800 render of a sphere with simple materials should be fine.

Let's start by checking the Blender instance and version, and whether the MCP server is running. Then create the scene.

Steps:
1. Inspect scene, version, render engines.
2. Build texture image via numpy: 2048x1024.
   - Land polygons in lat/lon. Need a set of polygons. Let me write down approximations.

Actually, another thought: I could procedurally generate a plausible "Earth-like" planet with a land mask from noise, which looks gorgeous but not Earth. The message "our pale blue dot" needs to be Earth. But a stylized planet with a realistic look is fine if it's clearly Earth. Let me do actual continent polygons; rough but recognizable.

Let me define coastline polygons as (lon, lat) lists. I'll write a helper to rasterize polygons using matplotlib? Not available. Use numpy + a point-in-polygon test over a 2048x1024 grid = 2M points × polygons (say 300 points) — too slow in pure Python (600M ops). Use a scanline fill for each polygon in radians: for each row, compute intersections; that's fast. Or use PIL? Not available (Blender's Python may include no PIL). Blender has numpy though. I can rasterize polygons to a 2048x1024 boolean mask with a per-row scanline algorithm in Python: for each row (1024) and each polygon (~10-30 points), compute intersections: 1024*300 = 300k, fine. Then also smooth.

Alternatively, use Blender's texture painting? No.

Scanline approach:
```
for each polygon:
  for each lat row y:
    lat = ...
    xs = []
    for each edge (lon1,lat1)-(lon2,lat2):
      if (lat1 > lat) != (lat2 > lat):
        xs.append(lon1 + (lat-lat1)*(lon2-lon1)/(lat2-lat1))
    xs.sort()

def periodic_bilinear(grid, H, W):
    gh, gw = grid.shape
    out = np.empty((H, W), np.float32)
    ys = np.linspace(0, gh-1, H)
    y0 = np.floor(ys).astype(int); y1=(y0+1)%gh; fy=ys-y0
    # first interpolate x for each row
    xs = np.linspace(0, gw-1, W, endpoint=False)
    x0 = np.floor(xs).astype(int); x1=(x0+1)%gw; fx=xs-x0
    rows = grid[:, x0]*(1-fx) + grid[:, x1]*fx
    out = rows[y0]*(1-fy)[:,None] + rows[y1]*fy[:,None]
    return out

def fbm(seed, octaves, base=6, H=1024, W=2048):
    out = np.zeros((H,W), np.float32)
    amp=1; norm=0
    for o in range(octaves):
        sw = base*(2**o); sh = max(2, sw//2)
        g = rng.normal(size=(sh, sw))
        out += amp*periodic_bilinear(g, H, W)
        norm += amp; amp*=0.5
    return out/norm
```

```python
W, H = 2048, 1024
rng = np.random.default_rng(7)

def periodic_up(grid, H, W):
    gh, gw = grid.shape
    xs = np.linspace(0, gw, W, endpoint=False)
    x0 = np.floor(xs).astype(np.int32)
    x1 = (x0+1) % gw
    fx = xs - x0
    rows = grid[:, x0]*(1-fx) + grid[:, x1]*fx  # (gh, W)
    ys = np.linspace(0, gh-1, H)
    y0 = np.floor(ys).astype(np.int32)
    y1 = np.minimum(y0+1, gh-1)
    fy = ys - y0
    return rows[y0]*(1-fy)[:,None] + rows[y1]*fy[:,None]

def fbm(seed, octaves=5, base_w=6, base_h=3, H=H, W=W, gain=0.5):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    out = np.zeros((H,W), np.float32)
    amp = 1.0; norm = 0.0
    for o in range(octaves):
        gw = base_w * (2**o)
        gh = max(2, base_h * (2**o))
        g = rng.normal(size=(gh, gw)).astype(np.float32)
        out += amp * periodic_up(g, H, W)
        norm += amp; amp *= gain
    out /= norm
    # normalize
    out -= out.min(); out /= out.max()
    return out
```

"""
PALE BLUE DOT / THE OVERVIEW
A procedural Earth built entirely in Blender.

Concept: the single most perspective-changing object ever seen by human eyes.
A portrait of the only home we have: no borders, one thin atmosphere, one moon.
"""
import bpy
import bmesh
import math
import os
import numpy as np
from mathutils import Vector

ROOT = os.getcwd()
TEX = os.path.join(ROOT, "tex")
OUT = os.path.join(ROOT, "output")
os.makedirs(TEX, exist_ok=True)
os.makedirs(OUT, exist_ok=True)

W, H = 2048, 1024
rng = np.random.default_rng(20261030)

# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# helpers
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

def smoothstep(e0, e1, x):
    t = np.clip((x - e0) / (e1 - e0), 0.0, 1.0)
    return t * t * (3.0 - 2.0 * t)


def periodic_up(grid, h, w):
    """bilinear upsample of a coarse field, periodic in x"""
    gh, gw = grid.shape
    xs = np.linspace(0.0, gw, w, endpoint=False)
    x0 = np.floor(xs).astype(np.int32)
    x1 = (x0 + 1) % gw
    fx = (xs - x0).astype(np.float32)
    rows = grid[:, x0] * (1.0 - fx)[None, :] + grid[:, x1] * fx[None, :]
    ys = np.linspace(0.0, gh - 1.0, h)
    y0 = np.floor(ys).astype(np.int32)
    y1 = np.minimum(y0 + 1, gh - 1)
    fy = (ys - y0).astype(np.float32)
    return rows[y0] * (1.0 - fy)[:, None] + rows[y1] * fy[:, None]


def fbm(seed, octaves=6, base_w=6, base_h=3, h=H, w=W, gain=0.5):
    r = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    out = np.zeros((h, w), np.float32)
    amp = 1.0
    norm = 0.0
    for o in range(octaves):
        gw = base_w * (2 ** o)
        gh = max(2, base_h * (2 ** o))
        g = r.normal(size=(gh, gw)).astype(np.float32)
        out += amp * periodic_up(g, h, w)
        norm += amp
        amp *= gain
    out /= norm
    out -= out.min()
    out /= max(out.max(), 1e-6)
    return out


def box_blur(a, rx, ry=None):
    if ry is None:
        ry = rx
    h, w = a.shape
    # horizontal wrap
    pad = np.pad(a, ((0, 0), (rx, rx)), mode="wrap")
    c = np.cumsum(pad, axis=1, dtype=np.float64)
    c = np.concatenate([np.zeros((h, 1)), c], axis=1)
    a = (c[:, 2 * rx + 1:] - c[:, :-(2 * rx + 1)]) / (2 * rx + 1)
    # vertical edge
    pad = np.pad(a, ((ry, ry), (0, 0)), mode="edge")
    c = np.cumsum(pad, axis=0, dtype=np.float64)
    c = np.concatenate([np.zeros((1, w)), c], axis=0)
    a = (c[2 * ry + 1:, :] - c[:-(2 * ry + 1), :]) / (2 * ry + 1)
    return a.astype(np.float32)


def save_image(name, arr, colorspace="sRGB", alpha=False, path=None):
    """arr is (H, W, 3) float or (H, W, 4) if alpha"""
    h, w = arr.shape[:2]
    if arr.shape[2] == 3:
        a = np.concatenate([arr, np.ones((h, w, 1), np.float32)], axis=2)
    else:
        a = arr
    img = bpy.data.images.new(name, width=w, height=h, alpha=True)
    img.pixels.foreach_set(np.ascontiguousarray(a, dtype=np.float32).ravel())
    img.colorspace_settings.name = colorspace
    if alpha:

    img.filepath_raw = path

def fill_poly(poly, value):
    n = len(poly)
    for j in range(H):
        lat = -90.0 + (j + 0.5) / H * 180.0
        xs = []
        for k in range(n):
            x1, y1 = poly[k]
            x2, y2 = poly[(k + 1) % n]
            if (y1 > lat) != (y2 > lat):
                xs.append(x1 + (lat - y1) * (x2 - x1) / (y2 - y1))
        if not xs:
            continue
        xs.sort()
        for a, b in zip(xs[0::2], xs[1::2]):
            i0 = int((a + 180.0) / 360.0 * W)
            i1 = int((b + 180.0) / 360.0 * W)
            i0 = max(0, min(W, i0))
            i1 = max(0, min(W, i1))
            if i1 > i0:
                land[j, i0:i1] = value


for name, poly in POLYS.items():
    fill_poly(poly, 1.0)

# Antarctica: a wavy cap

    fill_poly(poly, 0.0)

# close the dateline seam in the mask

land = box_blur(land, 1)
land = smoothstep(0.44, 0.56, land)

# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# earth colour / clouds / normal / roughness

n2 = fbm(102, 6, 8, 4)          # medium
n3 = fbm(103, 5, 24, 12)        # fine

deep = np.array([0.008, 0.035, 0.115], np.float32)
mid = np.array([0.012, 0.105, 0.235], np.float32)

ocean = ocean * (1 - 0.45 * smoothstep(0.0, 1.0, n3)[..., None]) + deep[None, None, :] * 0.45 * n3[..., None]

coast_broad = np.clip(4.0 * box_blur(land, 7) * (1.0 - box_blur(land, 7)), 0.0, 1.0)
shelf = np.clip(0.6 * coast + 0.9 * coast_broad * (1.0 - land), 0.0, 1.0)
ocean = ocean * (1 - shelf[..., None]) + shallow[None, None, :] * shelf[..., None] * (0.45 + 0.55 * n2[..., None])

green = np.array([0.055, 0.15, 0.042], np.float32)
lush = np.array([0.10, 0.255, 0.065], np.float32)

ice_sea = smoothstep(68.0, 80.0, lat_abs + 10.0 * (n1 - 0.5))

stars += milky[..., None] * np.array([0.030, 0.036, 0.052], np.float32)
# faint dust
dust = fbm(402, 5, 18, 9, h=SH, w=SW)
stars += (dust[..., None] ** 3) * band[..., None] * np.array([0.04, 0.035, 0.03], np.float32)

srng = np.random.default_rng(9090)
nstars = 15000
sx = srng.integers(0, SW, nstars)
sy = srng.integers(0, SH, nstars)
bright = (srng.random(nstars) ** 3.2) * 1.4 + 0.05
warm = srng.random(nstars)
for i in range(nstars):
    x = int(sx[i]); y = int(sy[i])
    b = bright[i]
    if warm[i] < 0.18:
        c = np.array([1.0, 0.82, 0.62], np.float32)
    elif warm[i] > 0.88:
        c = np.array([0.65, 0.80, 1.0], np.float32)
    else:
        c = np.array([1.0, 0.98, 0.94], np.float32)
    for dy in (-1, 0, 1):
        for dx in (-1, 0, 1):
            w = 1.0 if (dx == 0 and dy == 0) else (0.42 if abs(dx) + abs(dy) == 1 else 0.18)
            yy = (y + dy) % SH
            xx = (x + dx) % SW
            stars[yy, xx] = np.maximum(stars[yy, xx], c * b * w)

def uv_sphere(name, radius, segments, rings, img_uv=None):
    bpy.ops.mesh.primitive_uv_sphere_add(segments=segments, ring_count=rings, radius=radius,
                                         location=(0, 0, 0))
    ob = bpy.context.object
    ob.name = name
    me = ob.data
    me.name = name
    me.shade_smooth()
    # explicit equirectangular UVs with seam correction
    uvl = me.uv_layers.new(name="UVMap")
    for poly in me.polygons:
        idx = list(poly.loop_indices)
        us = []
        for li in idx:
            v = me.vertices[me.loops[li].vertex_index].co
            u = math.atan2(v.y, v.x) / (2 * math.pi) + 0.5
            w = math.asin(max(-1.0, min(1.0, v.z / radius))) / math.pi + 0.5
            uvl.data[li].uv = (u, w)
            us.append(u)
        if max(us) - min(us) > 0.5:
            for li in idx:
                uv = uvl.data[li].uv
                if uv.x < 0.5:
                    uv.x += 1.0
    return ob

def new_mat(name):
    m = bpy.data.materials.new(name)
    m.use_nodes = True
    nt = m.node_tree
    for n in list(nt.nodes):
        nt.nodes.remove(n)
    out = nt.nodes.new("ShaderNodeOutputMaterial")
    out.location = (600, 0)
    bsdf = nt.nodes.new("ShaderNodeBsdfPrincipled")
    bsdf.location = (250, 0)
    nt.links.new(bsdf.outputs["BSDF"], out.inputs["Surface"])
    return m, nt, bsdf

"""Final renders + GLB export for PALE BLUE DOT."""
import bpy
import os
import math
from mathutils import Vector

ROOT = os.getcwd()
OUT = os.path.join(ROOT, "output")
os.makedirs(OUT, exist_ok=True)

scene = bpy.context.scene
earth = bpy.data.objects["Earth"]
clouds = bpy.data.objects["Clouds"]
atmo = bpy.data.objects["Atmosphere"]
moon = bpy.data.objects["Moon"]

# hero camera (Earth portrait; moon is out of frame)
cam = bpy.data.objects["HeroCam"]
cam.location = (0.55, -5.00, 1.20)
cam.data.lens = 55
scene.camera = cam

scene.render.engine = "CYCLES"
scene.cycles.device = "GPU"
scene.cycles.samples = 96
scene.cycles.use_denoising = True
scene.cycles.use_adaptive_sampling = True
scene.cycles.adaptive_threshold = 0.015
scene.render.resolution_x = 1600
scene.render.resolution_y = 1200
scene.render.resolution_percentage = 100
scene.render.image_settings.file_format = "JPEG"
scene.render.image_settings.quality = 93
scene.render.filepath = os.path.join(OUT, "the_overview.jpg")
moon.hide_render = False

# ---------------- hero ----------------
scene.render.filepath = os.path.join(OUT, "the_overview.jpg")
bpy.ops.render.render(write_still=True)
print("hero done", os.path.getsize(scene.render.filepath))

# ---------------- wide (Earth + Moon) ----------------
moon.hide_render = False
wide_data = bpy.data.cameras.new("WideCam")
wide_data.lens = 50
wide_data.sensor_width = 36
wide_data.clip_start = 0.05
wide_data.clip_end = 2000
wide = bpy.data.objects.new("WideCam", wide_data)
scene.collection.objects.link(wide)
wide.location = (0.4, -9.30, 2.50)
target = bpy.data.objects["Target"]
target.location = (0, 0, 0.10)
tc = wide.constraints.new("TRACK_TO")
tc.target = target
tc.track_axis = "TRACK_NEGATIVE_Z"
tc.up_axis = "UP_Y"
scene.camera = wide
scene.render.filepath = os.path.join(OUT, "the_blue_dot.jpg")
bpy.ops.render.render(write_still=True)
print("wide done", os.path.getsize(scene.render.filepath))

# ---------------- export ----------------
scene.camera = cam
for ob in bpy.data.objects:
    ob.select_set(False)
for ob in (earth, clouds, atmo, moon):
    ob.select_set(True)
bpy.context.view_layer.objects.active = earth
glb_path = os.path.join(OUT, "pale_blue_dot.glb")
bpy.ops.export_scene.gltf(
    filepath=glb_path,
    export_format="GLB",
    use_selection=True,
    export_apply=True,
    export_yup=True,
    export_draco_mesh_compression_enable=False,
    export_meshopt_compression_enable=False,
)
print("glb", os.path.getsize(glb_path))
bpy.ops.wm.save_as_mainfile(filepath=os.path.join(ROOT, "pale_blue_dot_final.blend"))
print("FINAL OK")

content.text:
Made **“The Overview”** — a portrait of Earth as the one borderless home we all share: the view that reliably changes how people see the world.

**Built in Blender (procedurally, no external assets):**
- Hand-constructed equirectangular land/ocean map with recognizable continents, continental shelves, deserts, forests, ice caps, and a subtle relief normal map
- Separate semi-transparent cloud layer
- Thin blue atmosphere shell plus a render-only atmospheric rim glow
- Cratered Moon, procedural starfield, sun/fill lighting, and a soft bloom compositor
- Earth/Moon scene exported as a self-contained GLB with embedded textures

**Published in `./output/`:**
- `pale_blue_dot.glb` — 6.4 MB interactive model (Earth, clouds, atmosphere, Moon)
- `the_overview.jpg` — 1600×1200 hero portrait
- `the_blue_dot.jpg` — 1600×1200 Earth-and-Moon wide view

The piece is meant to do what the overview effect does: make the planet feel singular, fragile, and shared.
